draft.title: Types of adaptations
card: An adaptation is a trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment. Adaptations build up in a population over many generations through natural selection.
Structural
a physical feature of the body, such as the thick blubber of a seal or the sharp claws of an eagle.
Physiological
an internal process, such as a snake making venom or a mammal sweating to lose heat.
Behavioural
an action an organism takes, such as birds migrating or a lizard basking in the sun to warm up.
draft.remember: Adaptations can be what an organism has, what its body does inside, or what it does.

a.q: A frog living in a cold region produces a chemical in its blood that stops its cells from freezing. What type of adaptation is this?
opts: Physiological
Structural
Behavioural
Acquired
a.why: The chemical is made by an internal process in the body, so it is physiological. It is not structural, because it is not a physical body feature such as fur or claws, and the frog is not choosing an action.
a.clue: Is it a body part, an internal process or an action?

b.q: Which of these is a behavioural adaptation?
opts: A meerkat standing upright to watch for hawks
A camel storing fat in its hump
A cactus having a thick, waxy skin
A desert rat making very concentrated urine
b.why: Standing up to watch for predators is an action the animal takes, so it is behavioural. Storing fat in a hump is tempting, but the hump is a physical body feature, so it is structural. The waxy skin is structural and the concentrated urine is physiological.
b.clue: Look for the option where the organism does something.

b.best: A meerkat standing upright to watch for hawks

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'the frog is not choosing an action', which suggests behavioural adaptations are chosen. Many behaviours, such as migration, are innate. The card defines behavioural simply as 'an action an organism takes', so the why should use that wording.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate, and each question has one clear answer. The only issue is minor: why (a) says behavioural adaptations are 'chosen', which could mislead students about innate behaviours.
